extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent attorneys, patent examiners, law students, and interested public seeking to understand novelty under the EPC
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on assessing whether subject-matter is novel under the European Patent Convention (Article 54 EPC), including what counts as the state of the art, exceptions, and relevant case-law principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty requirement (Article 54 EPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention can be patented only if it is new. An invention is considered to be new if it does not form part of the state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose of Article 54(1) EPC is to prevent the state of the art being patented again. Novelty is a prerequisite for patentability under the EPC.

rubrics_metrics.name: State of the art (Article 54(2) EPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of the art shall be held to comprise everything made available to the public by means of a written or oral description, by use, or in any other way, before the date of filing of the European patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The state of the art under the EPC is absolute: even disclosure to a single person under no obligation of secrecy suffices; the theoretical possibility of unrestricted access to information can render it available to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enabling disclosure / reproducibility requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject-matter in a disclosure can only be regarded as having been made available to the public ... if the information given is sufficient to enable the skilled person, at the relevant date ... to practise the technical teaching which is the subject of the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prior disclosure only destroys novelty if the teaching it contains is reproducible. References: Guidelines for Examination in the EPO (enabling disclosure) and case law on reproducibility (e.g., Legal Research Service, 'Reproducibility of the content of the disclosure').

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The disclosure of a prior art document is regarded as encompassing not only its explicit disclosure but also 'everything that the skilled person would inherently understand when reading the document'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit disclosure means no more than the clear and unambiguous consequence of what is explicitly mentioned. Implicit features that the skilled person would directly derive are taken into account for novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 54(3) EPC — prior-filed European applications as prior art for novelty only
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 54(3) EPC includes 'the content of European patent applications as filed, the dates of filing of which are prior to the date referred to in paragraph 2 and which were published on or after that date' in the state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a notional extension meant to address conflicting prior rights; documents under Article 54(3) EPC are considered for novelty but are not to be considered in deciding on inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-prejudicial disclosures (Article 55 EPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 55 EPC provides two situations in which a disclosure before filing might not be regarded as part of the state of the art under Article 54 EPC: (1) an evident abuse 'in relation to the applicant or his legal predecessor', and (2) disclosure of an invention 'at an official, or officially recognised, international exhibition' falling within the terms of the Paris Convention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are narrow exceptions to absolute novelty that may render an otherwise pre-filing disclosure non-prejudicial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific disclosure vs generic claim principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A specific disclosure does take away the novelty of a generic claim embracing that disclosure, whereas a generic disclosure does not normally take away the novelty of any specific example falling within that disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: a disclosure of copper takes away the novelty of 'metal' as a generic concept, but a generic disclosure (e.g., of a general teaching) normally does not deprive a specific embodiment of novelty. Case law and Guidelines support this distinction (see decisions T 651/91, T 776/07).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal fiction of Article 54(4) and (5) EPC — new medical/therapeutic uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 54(4) and (5) EPC acknowledge the notional novelty of substances or compositions even when they are as such already comprised in the state of the art, provided they are claimed for a new use in a method which Article 53(c) EPC excludes as such from patent protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows, for example, first medical use claims to be treated as novel and to receive broad protection covering any use in a medical method even if only one specific use is disclosed (see case law T 128/82, T 36/83 and G 2/08). This principle complements Article 53(c)'s exclusion of medical methods from patentability of methods (not products).
